chapter: Dizzy, Chano Pozo and Afro-Cuban jazz
title: Teaching Dizzy rhythms in the Calloway band
summary: Bauza hums Afro-Cuban rhythms to Dizzy backstage, and Dizzy later sits in at the Park Plaza.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x:
Okay, I would like to -- we started to talk about Gillespie, but I would like to get back into Dizzy Gillespie. You talked earlier about how you got to (inaudible) and the Cab Calloway band. But if you can just start talking about the importance of Gillespie and Afro-Cuban music and how he got involved with it.

I remember your once telling me that he was jamming with you once or twice.

Well, way before that, see. When I got Dizzy into Calloway band, he was my roommate. In the back of his mind he had -- in the back of his mind he had something to improve the way of playing, something that he figured would be a volume rhythm-wise but what he was thinking of doing harmonic-wise.

First he had a (inaudible) harmonic-wise, because the average musician, he liked what he was doing. So he had to simplify everything. He went out of key, and he played funny notes and, you know, a whole lot of crazy things. So he had enough trouble trying to convince people in that. So when we really were close, we were together, tried to find out what can we add to the things to create where we want to create. And so we start fooling around with Cozy Cole behind the stage.

I show rhythms. He always practice his sticks, always between shows. I used to hum rhythms to him, and he
trying to play with a stick.

Yeah. So this was getting into all (inaudible) more, more, more and more every day. So one day I said to him, why don't you (inaudible), why don't you write me something, see how you focus this thing, give me the -- give me the one arrangement.
Do you remember what it was?

(inaudible). So anyhow, we were fooling around with an idea, and we talk with -- so the first opportunity he had after I left the band, he came a couple of times, came to the Park Plaza, where I was playing with my band. He come in there and sit down.

The Park Plaza was 110 and Fifth Avenue. So he used to come around there. And he'd sit down and play in the band. But the same time the people in the dance say, that trumpet player go off key and everything. You know what I mean. So I say, oh, well, you people don't understand what a man's trying to produce. You know what I mean.
Yeah. So the principal tune he had right after he left Calloway, came to see me, said, Mario, I've been
keeping toying with an idea. And I wanted you to help me to get some people who can play (inaudible). You see, he had a goal. So that's how he really got into this.
